noteBlocks.lede: Sometimes the unknown is the power itself. You cannot divide a power away, so the equation looks stuck. Taking logarithms of both sides brings the index down to the front, and what is left is an ordinary linear equation you already know how to solve.
can: Take logarithms of both sides and bring the index down with brackets
Expand, collect the x terms on one side and factorise to reach x
Keep full accuracy until the last step and answer to the accuracy asked for

noteBlocks.text: When the unknown has climbed into the power

noteBlocks.md:
$2^{x} = 40$ looks like nothing you can rearrange. Dividing by $2$ does not touch the $x$, because the $x$ is an index rather than a multiplier.
A logarithm is the tool that moves it. Take logs of both sides and the power law turns $\log 2^{x}$ into $x \log 2$, so the $x$ becomes an ordinary factor and the equation becomes linear.

noteBlocks.prompt: One tap to begin. In the picture above, $2^{x} = 40$ becomes $x \log 2 = \log 40$. Which law of logarithms did that?
noteBlocks.explain: $\log a^{n} = n \log a$ is the power law. It is the only one that moves an index, and it is the first line of every question of this kind.

noteBlocks.md:
Solve $5^{3x - 2} = 40$.
**Step 1.** Take logs of both sides.
**Step 2.** The power law brings the whole index down, in brackets: $(3x - 2) \log 5 = \log 40$.
**Step 3.** Divide by $\log 5$, then tidy the linear equation.
**Step 4.** Evaluate once, at the end: $x = 1.43$ to two decimal places.

noteBlocks.title: Why taking logs frees the unknown
noteBlocks.md: Every $\log$ in these lines is just a number, so once the index is down at the front the equation is linear in $x$ and the ordinary rules apply. That is the whole purpose of the first line: it changes what kind of equation you are looking at.

noteBlocks.prompt: Working on $5^{3x - 2} = 40$: taking logs and dividing gives $3x - 2 = \frac{\log 40}{\log 5}$. What is $x$, correct to two decimal places?

noteBlocks.md:
The index is a whole expression, so all of it comes down together and all of it needs a bracket: $(4x + 1) \log 2$, never $4x + 1 \log 2$.
Without the bracket the logarithm multiplies only the last term, and the equation being solved is no longer the one that was set. It is the single most reported slip on this topic.

noteBlocks.md: Most candidates knew to take logarithms and the question was answered well. The marks that went were careless: the brackets left off the index, and bases other than ten producing extra slips. Isolating the unknown was the hurdle for everyone else.

noteBlocks.prompt: Taking logs of $2^{4x + 1} = 7^{x + 3}$ gives which line?
noteBlocks.explain: Each whole index comes down in front of its own logarithm, inside a bracket. Without the brackets the logarithms multiply only the constants.

noteBlocks.md:
With logarithms on both sides there are two $x$ terms. Expand each bracket, move the $x$ terms to one side and the numbers to the other, then factorise $x$ out.
Every $\log$ here is just a number, so treat them exactly as you would treat any letters in a linear equation. The sign is what goes wrong: a term that crosses the equals sign changes sign.

noteBlocks.why: The same four moves worked through on several equations, with the brackets written every time.

noteBlocks.prompt: Solve $3^{x} = 11$, giving your answer correct to two decimal places. Keep the logarithms in the calculator until the final step.
noteBlocks.explain: $x = \frac{\log 11}{\log 3} = 2.182658$, which is $2.18$. Rounding each logarithm first would give $2.17$.

noteBlocks.md:
Recognise that an unknown in the index needs logarithms, not division.
Take logs of both sides and bring each whole index down inside a bracket.
Expand, collect the $x$ terms on one side and factorise $x$ out.
Divide and evaluate in one calculator step at the end.
Spot when both sides share a base, and solve by equating indices instead.

This is a standard $4$ or $5$ mark part, usually the second half of a logarithm question. The first mark is taking logs of both sides; the last is the answer to two decimal places. Stuck? Write the logs of both sides and bring each index down in a bracket — that line alone earns the first two marks, whatever happens afterwards.

parts.workedSolution:
Taking logs: $\log 2^{x} = \log 40$, so $x \log 2 = \log 40$.
$x = \frac{\log 40}{\log 2} = 5.321928$.
To two decimal places, $x = 5.32$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $40 \div 2$. An index is not a multiplier, so it cannot be divided away; taking logarithms is what frees the $x$.
The two logarithms have been subtracted where the method divides them. From $x \log 2 = \log 40$ you divide, which gives $5.32$.

findTheMistake.stem: Cara was asked to solve $7^{3x - 1} = 200$ correct to two decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 1 is right: logarithms of both sides is always the first move.
Line 2 brings the index down without a bracket, so $\log 7$ multiplies only the $1$ and no longer multiplies the $3x$. Everything after that solves a different equation, which is why the answer is out by more than a rounding.
The line should read $(3x - 1) \log 7 = \log 200$, and then $x = 1.24$.
findTheMistake.feedback: Taking logarithms of both sides is the right first move and it earns its mark. The bracket is what the rest depends on: the index is one expression, so all of it multiplies the logarithm. Write the bracket as you bring the index down, every time, and the rest is a linear equation you can already do.

prompts.prompt: Give the first two lines of solving an equation with the unknown in the index.
prompts.answer: Take logarithms of both sides, then use the power law to bring each whole index down in front of its logarithm, inside a bracket.

prompts.prompt: Why must the index be written in a bracket when it comes down?
prompts.answer: Because the whole index multiplies the logarithm. Without the bracket only the constant is multiplied, and the equation being solved is no longer the one that was set.

prompts.prompt: With logarithms on both sides, how is $x$ found?
prompts.answer: Expand both brackets, move the $x$ terms to one side and the numbers to the other, factorise $x$ out, then divide.

prompts.prompt: From $x \log 2 = \log 40$, what is the next line, and what is it not?
prompts.answer: It is $x = \frac{\log 40}{\log 2}$, a quotient of the two logarithms. It is not $\log 40 - \log 2$, which is a different number.

prompts.prompt: When should the calculator be used in an indicial equation, and to what accuracy is the answer given?
prompts.answer: Only at the last step, on the whole expression at once. Give two decimal places unless the question says otherwise.

prompts.prompt: When can an indicial equation be solved without logarithms at all?
prompts.answer: When both sides can be written as powers of the same base. Then the indices are equal and the equation is linear at once.
